mediaItem.itemTitle: Jason Flom with Frederick Willie Kearse
mediaItem.summaryNotes: This episode of Wrongful Conviction features the story of Frederick Willie Kurz, who was wrongfully convicted of murder in Brooklyn, NY, in 1995 and served 28 years in prison.  The podcast details the corrupt practices of the 75th Precinct in the 1990s, highlighting how pressure to close cases led to fabricated evidence and coerced witness testimonies.  Frederick recounts his life before and after his wrongful conviction, emphasizing the lack of proper legal representation and his self-education in law while incarcerated.  Key factors contributing to his wrongful conviction included unreliable eyewitness testimony, flawed ballistics evidence, and ineffective defense counsel.  Despite evidence debunking the prosecution's case, Frederick was not fully exonerated but was released on parole in 2021 thanks to the efforts of the Parole Prep Project and a change in stance from the District Attorney's office. The episode underscores systemic issues within the criminal justice system and the long-lasting personal impact of wrongful convictions.

featuredIndividual.caseLocation: East New York, Brooklyn, New York City, NY
featuredIndividual.exonerationYear: Not exonerated, released on parole in December 2021.
featuredIndividual.crimeConvictedOf: Murder of Devon Brown, Attempted Murder of Ray Frazier, weapon possession, assault.
featuredIndividual.sentence: 20 years to life for murder, 8 1/3 to 25 years for attempted murder, 5 to 15 years for weapon possession, and 2 1/3 to 7 years for assault, all served consecutively to the 20 to life sentence.
contributingFactorsRaw: Eyewitness Misidentification: Greg Maloney and Barbara Garth provided unreliable and coerced eyewitness testimonies, which contradicted their initial statements to police.
Flawed Ballistics Evidence: Ballistics analysis was presented as a "perfect match," which is scientifically impossible and was not properly challenged by defense counsel.
Ineffective Assistance of Counsel:  Frederick's trial attorney, Stephen Shaken, provided inadequate representation, failing to challenge evidence and communicate effectively with his client.
Systemic Corruption: The 75th Precinct was known for corruption and pressure to close cases, leading to unethical police practices.
organizationsInvolvedRaw: Parole Prep Project: Assisted with parole application and post-release support.
Beldock Levine and Hoffman (law firm): Mark Cannon and previously Myron Beldock and Keith Schapansky for reinvestigation and legal representation post-conviction.
Freedom Agenda (mentioned as sponsor, advocating for Rikers Island closure)
innocenceLawyersRaw: Mark Cannon of Beldock Levine and Hoffman: Civil rights attorney who represented Frederick in his efforts towards exoneration.
Keith Schapansky (formerly with Beldock Levine and Hoffman):  Investigated the case prior to Mark Cannon.
Myron Beldock (Founding partner of Beldock Levine and Hoffman, now deceased): Initially reviewed Frederick's case letter and passed it to Keith Schapansky.
featuredIndividual.crossReference: Not specified if in exoneree database, needs to be checked.
featuredIndividual.narrativeOriginalCrime: On August 6, 1993, a drive-by shooting occurred in front of a bodega in East New York, Brooklyn.  A car drove up and fired shots, killing Devon Brown and injuring Ray Frazier. The police investigation focused on a suspect nicknamed "Guns."
keyEvidenceProsecutionRaw: Eyewitness testimony from Greg Maloney and Barbara Garth identifying Frederick as the shooter.
Ballistics evidence linking a gun found in a car Frederick was in a month later to casings from the crime scene.
featuredIndividual.trialDefenderNotes: Stephen Shaken, Frederick's trial lawyer, was described as providing ineffective counsel. He did not challenge the ballistics evidence effectively and had poor communication with Frederick.  The defense primarily relied on an alibi from a roommate in Boston, which was not compelling enough for the jury.
keyEvidenceExonerationRaw: Recantation of Greg Maloney: Admitted to being coerced by police and falsely identifying Frederick.
Testimony of Gavin Johnson: Knew Greg Maloney was not truthful and connected Frederick with Maloney for recantation.
Testimony of Donald Johnson (Gavin's brother): Corroborated inconsistencies in eyewitness accounts.
Unredacted DD-5 hospital reports: Showed Barbara Garth's initial statement contradicted her trial testimony about her location during the shooting, indicating perjury.
Expert testimony debunking ballistics evidence: Highlighted the flawed nature of the "perfect match" claim.
District Attorney's office letter of non-opposition to parole: Signaled a shift in their stance due to the evidence of wrongful conviction.
featuredIndividual.actualPerpetratorDetails: Not identified in the podcast transcript.

keyQuotesRaw: Michael Race (former 75th Precinct sergeant): "over the 750 murder investigations that he supervised at the 75th Precinct, only one was done correctly."

Frederick Willie Kurz: "I stood on a premise of I did not do this crime, and so many people I was with went through the same thing." "I have to keep a level mind to expose this system as much as I can."

Mark Cannon: "Willie should never have been convicted. And a large part of why he did get wrongfully convicted and stayed in jail for the 28 years is because he never got the representation he should have."
systemicIssuesRaw: Police Corruption and Pressure to Close Cases: The 75th Precinct's corrupt practices and focus on conviction rates over justice.
Ineffective Legal Representation:  Inadequate defense counsel failing to challenge flawed evidence and protect the rights of the accused.
Flawed Forensic Science:  Misuse and misrepresentation of ballistics evidence.
Coerced and Unreliable Eyewitness Testimony:  Police manipulation and pressure on witnesses.
Racial Disparities in the Justice System:  Mentioned by Frederick regarding the disproportionate impact on people of color.
Parole process challenges: Even after long sentences and evidence of wrongful conviction, parole can be difficult and re-traumatizing.
policyRecommendationsRaw: Implicit call for conviction integrity units to review cases like Frederick's.
Highlighted need for better legal representation for defendants, especially in marginalized communities.
Advocacy for criminal justice reform to address systemic issues.
Support for organizations like Parole Prep Project and Freedom Agenda.
personalNarrativeRaw: Frederick's resilience and determination to fight for his innocence despite facing immense adversity and trauma.
His focus on systemic issues rather than personal bitterness.
His commitment to helping others through the Parole Prep Project and archive-based creative art program.
The devastating impact of wrongful conviction on Frederick's life, family, and opportunities, including missed years with his daughter and difficulty finding employment post-release.
